findings.what: design.md blames the JSON naming policy for ?REFERENCE=x giving the key 'reference'. The serializer never camel-cases error keys, and the app's helper turns COLOUR into cOLOUR.
findings.why: Lines 64-65 say: 'That is the JSON naming policy applied to the key.' The repo contradicts this in four places. (1) Program.cs:50-56 sets no DictionaryKeyPolicy, and the Web defaults camel-case property names only, not dictionary keys. (2) The comment at PoliciesController.cs:93 says 'ValidationProblem() does not camel-case keys, so the wire name is spelled out'. (3) docs/qa/build-F4.md:269-273 records, measured over HTTP, that the key 'Amount' came back unchanged. (4) The only key rewrite is ValidationProblems.CamelCase (ValidationProblems.cs:25-26), which lower-cases only the first letter of each dotted segment. So an unknown '?COLOUR=x' comes back as 'cOLOUR', not camelCase. 'reference' most likely appears because ModelState matches keys case-insensitively and merges 'REFERENCE' with the entry for the bound route parameter 'reference'. No test pins this (no REFERENCE in tests/). The F2 QA note (docs/qa/build-F2.md:214-217) put the JSON-policy cause forward only as a guess ('That looks like…'), and design.md now states it as fact under 'Two details that surprise people'. An assessor who tries another upper-case key will see the doc is wrong, and David cannot defend the stated cause. Fix direction: state what the repo proves and nothing more (for example, say the key is reported as bound or as sent, with the first letter lower-cased), or remove the explanation.

findings.what: 'Every problem' is said to carry type /problems/{rule-id}, ruleId and traceId. 400, 413, 429, 500 and the concurrency 409 have no ruleId, and their type is not a rule id.
findings.why: The table at line 55 already says a 400 has no ruleId, so the doc contradicts itself. UnexpectedExceptionHandler.cs:36 gives a 500 the type rfc9110#section-15.6.1 with no ruleId. The concurrency 409 is /problems/concurrency with no ruleId (UnexpectedExceptionHandler.cs:49), and a 429 is /problems/rate-limited (Program.cs:157). The requirements line (requirements.md:121) covers only 'every rule violation'. Narrow the sentence to rule violations (404, 409, 422).

findings.what: 'Only merged code reaches them' overclaims. The trigger limits CI runs only, so a manual run of any branch reaches the self-hosted pools unless a branch control check exists. None is documented.
findings.why: azure-pipelines.yml:5-9 sets only the CI trigger and pr: none. Azure DevOps lets anyone with queue rights run a pipeline manually against any branch, and that branch's YAML then runs on policies-<env>-vnet with the service connections. Nothing in the repo or the one-time setup list adds a branch control check that limits the environment or connections to main. The sentence presents a control that is not there. Either say a branch control check (main only) is part of the one-time setup, or soften the claim.
